messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 68-year-old widowed man of African descent who has worked as a professional dancer and movement instructor for most of his adult life. He presented for psychological assessment approximately seven months after surviving a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, reporting a PCL-5 score of 67 and describing a daily life that has contracted dramatically since the crash.

The collision occurred on a busy urban intersection when a commercial truck ran a red light and struck the driver's side of Kwame's sedan at high speed. The impact was sudden and total — the shriek of tyres, the concussive roar of metal on metal, the shattering of glass, and then a period Kwame cannot account for. He was extracted by emergency services and hospitalised for several weeks with serious injuries. What haunts him now is not only what he remembers but what he cannot. He has the impression of only fragments: the moment before impact, a sensation of weightlessness, then fluorescent hospital lighting. The middle — the collision itself, the extraction, the first hours — remains inaccessible, a gap he cannot bridge no matter how deliberately he tries to reach into it. When he attempts to reconstruct the event, the memory resists him, yielding no coherent narrative he can hold from beginning to end. This fragmentation has itself become a source of dread, because the absence of a complete story means the worst possibilities — that he panicked, that he failed to act, that his body simply gave out — remain unrefuted in his mind.

That interpretive void has fed a set of beliefs that now organise much of Kwame's inner life. He has come to believe that he cannot trust himself to respond correctly in a crisis, a conviction that the gap in his memory seems to confirm every time he tries and fails to retrieve it. His body, which carried him through decades of demanding physical performance, now feels like an unreliable instrument — it was injured in a moment he cannot even recall, and he is no longer certain it will do what he needs it to do. He also carries a bitter sense that the traffic systems and municipal infrastructure that should have prevented the crash failed him entirely, a belief that has generalised into a broader suspicion of institutions and the built environment. These appraisals — of personal unreliability, bodily betrayal, and institutional failure — have in turn amplified his perception of the world as actively dangerous. He is certain that delays of any kind signal imminent harm: a slow-moving elevator, a traffic light that holds a beat too long, a delivery that does not arrive on time. Unexpected or loud sounds — a car door slamming in the street below, a sudden burst of music from a passing vehicle — send him into an immediate state of high alert that takes many minutes to subside. He insists on positioning himself with his back to a wall in any room, scanning for exits, a habit that has made him conspicuous and exhausted in equal measure.

Because his body and his judgment feel untrustworthy, and because the fragmented memory offers no reassurance that he coped well, Kwame has steadily withdrawn. He no longer goes out unless absolutely necessary. The studio where he taught movement classes — the physical space most central to his identity since his wife's death three years ago — has been entirely abandoned. He avoids the colleagues and students he once socialised with, unable to face their concern or the questions he could not answer. The avoidance has brought a kind of muted relief, but it has also sealed him inside a world where the threats he monitors are never disconfirmed, and where the hypervigilance that drove him indoors continues to intensify without correction. He has also found himself withdrawing from the early sessions of therapy, deliberately pushing away anything discussed in those meetings, as though examining the material might make the fragmented memory cohere into something even more unbearable.

What finally brought Kwame to seek more intensive help was a phone call from a former student asking whether he would consider returning to teach a single class. He realised he could not imagine walking through the studio door. He arrived at this assessment hoping, above all, to understand why his body and mind feel so foreign to him — and afraid, most deeply, that they always will.
